papers.selection_reason: Introduces a fixed-size recurrent memory mechanism (DeltaNet variant) for constant-memory recall, directly addressing memory efficiency and retention in agents.
papers.title: Constant-Memory Recall: Learned Associations in a Fixed Matrix State
papers.tldr: A small DeltaNet with 32 KiB of fixed recurrent matrix state recalls 32 learned key-value pairings with near-perfect accuracy, though capacity and efficiency remain unresolved.

papers.abstract: Reliable recovery of missing measurements is important for monitoring and analysis in energy time-series systems, where fine-grained measurements may contain sensitive temporal information. Diffusion models trained with differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) provide a promising framework for privacy-sensitive energy time-series imputation. Under cosine diffusion schedules, late timesteps correspond to low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions, where standard $\varepsilon$-prediction can induce large pre-clipping gradients. Such gradients are more likely to be clipped, reducing the retained optimization signal. The artificial intelligence (AI) contribution lies in formulating this objective--clipping interaction as an objective optimization problem under fixed-threshold DP-SGD and developing timestep-aware objective conditioning for diffusion-based energy time-series imputation. The method adopts $v$-prediction to mitigate late-timestep gradient amplification, uses static loss weighting as a uniform-scaling control, and introduces diffusion-schedule-aware dynamic weighting for stronger attenuation before clipping. For the engineering application, we evaluate the method on five real-world energy time-series datasets across random point missingness, contiguous block missingness, persistent outages, and multiple missing-data severities. Under matched DP-SGD settings, the proposed method consistently improves imputation utility over the $\varepsilon$-prediction baseline. Gradient diagnostics reveal lower upper-tail pre-clipping gradient norms, reduced clipping fractions, and stronger attenuation at late low-SNR timesteps, supporting the effectiveness of clipping-aware objective conditioning for energy time-series imputation.
authors: Huizhen Huang, Yu Li, Tao Huang, Chen Hou
bullets: Addresses privacy-sensitive recovery of missing energy measurements under DP-SGD.
Identifies large late-timestep gradients in ε-prediction as a source of signal loss from clipping.
Uses v-prediction, static loss weighting, and diffusion-schedule-aware dynamic weighting to control gradients.
Evaluated on five real-world datasets across point, block, persistent-outage, and varying-severity missingness.
The proposed approach consistently improves utility over ε-prediction and reduces gradient tail norms and clipping fractions.

papers.abstract: Visual-token compression for vision--language models is posed almost entirely as a selection problem: decide which tokens to keep and discard the rest. The criteria that work best rank tokens by the attention the language model pays them, which makes the ranking a function of the question being asked. That is invisible in a single-turn benchmark and decisive whenever a compressed representation is written once and read many times, as when it is cached across the turns of a conversation or transmitted between a device and a server. We take the other half of the classical transform-coding toolkit instead: keep every token and vary its rate. A transform code exposes each token's measured distortion--rate curve, and a fixed bit budget is distributed across tokens by exact integer rate--distortion optimisation on those curves. No text enters the pipeline, so one compressed representation serves any query. At equal bit budgets, on two datasets and two capacities, it preserves the model's output distribution and its answers better than uniform-rate coding, the closed-form water-fill and distortion-ranked pruning. It matches attention-ranked pruning on the question pruning was tuned for, and overtakes it once the compressed image must answer a different question about the same image.
authors: Hongbo Zhang, Zihao Yang, Liuyang Song, Daqian Yang, Haoyang Yao, Yan Wen, Zhengtao Yao
bullets: Problem: Attention-based token selection depends on the current question, limiting representations that are cached or reused across queries.
Method: Keep every visual token and distribute a fixed bit budget using exact integer rate–distortion optimisation over each token’s distortion–rate curve.
Scope: The compression pipeline uses no text, enabling one representation to serve multiple queries.
Results: Across two datasets and model capacities, it better preserves output distributions and answers than uniform-rate coding, water-filling, and distortion-ranked pruning.
It matches attention-ranked pruning on its tuned question and outperforms it when answering a different question about the same image.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in motion generation and whole-body tracking have enabled humanoid robots to execute increasingly diverse motions, yet the same motion capabilities may be requested repeatedly during continual deployment. Reliable reuse is challenging because intervening motions can change the robot's entry state, making previously successful motions unsafe to replay blindly. Meanwhile, validated capabilities accumulate during deployment, while bounded storage requires deciding which ones are worth retaining. To address these challenges, we present HumanoidTTT, a framework for test-time capability reuse in continual humanoid control. Specifically, we introduce Selective Full-Motion Reuse, which authorizes direct reuse of validated complete motions only from certified applicable entry states, allowing accepted reuse to bypass fresh generation. We further introduce Test-Time Capability Consolidation, which adapts which qualified capabilities persist in a bounded Full-Motion Store using subsequent deployment reuse as feedback. Experiments demonstrate zero unsafe accepts and a 16.4$\times$ end-to-end speedup over fresh generation, while online consolidation improves avoided generator calls by 13.2 per 200 requests over its frozen counterpart. Overall, HumanoidTTT enables reliable and efficient reuse of validated motion capabilities while adaptively retaining useful capabilities throughout continual deployment. Code: https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/HumanoidTTT. Website: https://aigeeksgroup.github.io/HumanoidTTT.
authors: Jingtai Yang, Yining Wu, Yanjun Li, Zeyu Zhang, Hao Tang
bullets: Addresses repeated motion requests under changing robot entry states and bounded storage.
Selective Full-Motion Reuse permits direct replay only from certified applicable entry states.
Test-Time Capability Consolidation updates the bounded motion store using deployment reuse feedback.
Experiments report zero unsafe accepts and a 16.4× end-to-end speedup over fresh generation.
Online consolidation avoids 13.2 more generator calls per 200 requests than a frozen store.

The intervening motion changes the robot state before A is requested again, so reuse begins from a changed valid entry state. When a Qualified Capability reaches a full Store, a Store-conditioned Double-DQN chooses SKIP or replacement of an existing entry and adapts online from subsequent deployment reuse utility.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have shown strong potential for video understanding and caption generation, but their performance may decline in specialized medical imaging domains such as echocardiography. This work introduces Gaussian Process Embedding Correction (GPEC), a modular and computationally efficient pre-LLM error-correction method that improves the visual representations used by VideoChat2 for cardiac ultrasound caption generation. GPEC is inserted between the visual projection layer and the language model and learns a residual correction that moves the projected visual representation toward an annotation-guided target. The target is constructed by converting structured video annotations into qualitative attributes, generating a fixed-format reference caption, and mapping it into the language-model embedding space. The correction is modeled using a sparse variational Gaussian Process with inducing points, natural-parameter variational updates, and a block-wise linear kernel, while the original VideoChat2 components remain frozen.The method is evaluated using representation-level, caption-level, content-oriented, and execution-time metrics by comparing the original VideoChat2 with VideoChat2 + GPEC under identical input and reference conditions. Results show improved caption similarity and content alignment after applying the proposed correction. Furthermore, GPEC adds less than 0.05 s of inference-time overhead per video in the evaluated setting. These findings indicate that GPEC can improve caption generation in specialized medical video domains with minimal computational cost, without requiring end-to-end fine-tuning of the pretrained multimodal backbone.
authors: Arefeh Rezaei
bullets: Addresses performance degradation of multimodal LLMs in specialized echocardiography captioning.
Learns an annotation-guided residual embedding correction using a sparse variational Gaussian Process with inducing points.
Operates modularly between the visual projection layer and language model while keeping VideoChat2 frozen.
Improves caption similarity and content alignment compared with the original VideoChat2 under matched conditions.
Adds less than 0.05 seconds of inference overhead per video in the evaluated setting.

Table 3: Content-oriented evaluation of generated captions on 25 test samples. Higher values indicate better performance.

papers.selection_reason: Improves MLLM-based cardiac video captioning via pre-LLM embedding correction; fits multimodal LLM and video understanding.
papers.title: GPEC: Efficient Pre-LLM Gaussian Process Embedding Correction for Cardiac Video Caption Generation
papers.tldr: GPEC efficiently corrects VideoChat2’s visual embeddings before language generation, improving cardiac ultrasound caption quality with minimal inference overhead and no end-to-end backbone fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Biological neurons achieve computational diversity through specialized types: tonic, bursting, adapting, and fast-spiking cells coexist within the same circuit. Artificial neural networks, by contrast, apply a single activation function uniformly to all nodes, which limits what they can represent. We show that this uniformity creates hard limits for evolutionary search: across sparse evolved substrates, monotonic functions fail to solve parity beyond its smallest instance, XOR, while a single oscillatory unit suffices at all tested scales. The gap is one of search and sparsity, not representation: monotonic networks can represent parity with a modest number of hidden units, and gradient descent recovers that solution. We evolve, to our knowledge for the first time in indirect encoding, per-node activation function assignments from an 18-function palette across more than 4,500 experimental runs spanning Boolean logic, regression, and spatial classification. Testing each of the 18 functions individually on Parity-4 reveals a three-tier solvability structure: oscillatory functions achieve 100%, intermediate functions 6.7-80%, and all 9 monotonic functions 0%. This divide is not universal. Recurrence collapses it, and gradient descent inverts it entirely, showing that the barrier is specific to evolutionary search in sparse substrates. What activation functions a network can use, beyond its topology and weights, determines what evolutionary search can solve. Indirect encoding discovers heterogeneous per-node activation assignments unlikely to be chosen by hand.
authors: Romain Claret, Michael O'Neill, Paul Cotofrei, Kilian Stoffel
bullets: Uniform monotonic activations fail to evolve solutions for parity beyond XOR, while a single oscillatory unit solves all tested scales.
The limitation is primarily evolutionary search and sparsity—not representational capacity, since monotonic networks can represent parity and gradient descent can find such solutions.
Across 18 functions, Parity-4 shows three solvability tiers: oscillatory functions reach 100%, intermediate functions 6.7–80%, and all monotonic functions 0%.
Recurrence removes the activation-function divide, while gradient descent reverses it, indicating the effect is specific to sparse evolutionary search.
Indirect encoding evolves heterogeneous activation assignments across Boolean logic, regression, and spatial classification tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: System pipeline. The activation palette, through the per-node selection mechanism, assigns each node its own activation function; the CPPN genome (NEAT) is decoded into a substrate carrying these per-node activations, the substrate is evaluated for fitness, and NEAT selection closes the evolutionary loop. Three assignment methods determine how CPPN output maps to function selection.

Figure 2: Oscillatory structure predicts solvability. Local extrema count in [−5, 5] vs Parity-4 solve rate (N=30) for all 18 activation functions. Functions with more local extrema achieve higher solve rates. The two outliers at 2 extrema reflect extrema amplitude: band pass has deep signreversing extrema (100%), while integrate has shallow perturbations of a monotonic trend (0%).

Table 4: Assignment method comparison on Two Spirals (N=30; depth 3). CPPN-output significantly outperforms the other methods; weight-interpretation gives no gain over the uniform baseline. cppn output k = CPPN-output over a k-function palette (4: monotonic only; 6: adds sin, gauss).

Table 1: 18 activation functions and their individual Parity-4 results (Per-Function Ablation; N=30 seeds; 300 gen max). The solvability boundary follows oscillatory structure: functions with local extrema solve parity; 9 strictly monotonic functions never solve.

Table 9: Cross-problem comparison for representative functions. The three-tier solvability structure replicates on problems requiring non-monotonic decision surfaces (Parity-4, Circles) and vanishes on smooth problems (Sine, Step). All cells N=30. % = solve rate; Gen = median generations to solve.

Table 2: Parity scaling: sin vs tanh (N=30 seeds each; population 150; 100 gen max). Sin achieves 100% across all sizes; tanh degrades monotonically. Percentages are solve rates (replications reaching the threshold).
Table 5: Palette size vs convergence speed (N=30 seeds per size; Parity-4; all 100% success).

Table 8: Recurrence on concentric circles (N=30 each; solve threshold 0.90). Opposite to parity, recurrence degrades most functions; only osc adapt stays at 100%. FF% = feedforward solve rate; Full Rec% = full recurrence; Hidden-only% = recurrence on hidden-to-hidden connections only.
Table 7: Connection type decomposition (tanh on Parity-4, N=30, 300 gen max, pop 150; solve threshold 0.95). Each row adds one connection type to hidden-to-hidden (h-to-h) as base.
Table 3: Population reshapes the dynamics but not the oscillatory divide (Parity-4, N=30 per cell, 100 gen max). Sin solves 100% at every size; tanh 0% at every size. Percentages are solve rates.

Table 6: Feedforward vs recurrent topology on Parity-4 (both N=30, 300 gen max, pop 150; solve threshold 0.95). Recurrence partially collapses the divide: oscillatory functions remain at 100%; bounded monotonic partially solve; unbounded/linear remain near 0%. % = solve rate.

Table 10: Gradient-trained MLP baseline (Adam, lr=0.01, 5,000 epochs max, N=30). The divide progressively reverses: tanh maintains 100% through Parity-8; sin degrades to 0%. Increasing h does not help sin; it makes it worse on Parity-6 (66.7%→46.7%).

papers.selection_reason: Investigates evolutionary search limits for per-node activation functions in indirect encoding. Relevant to 'Robot Learning and Manipulation' as it explores novel evolutionary architectures for control.
papers.title: Per-Node Activation Function Evolution in Indirectly Encoded Substrates: Solvability, Limits, and Emergent Diversity
papers.tldr: Evolving different activation functions per node can overcome search and sparsity barriers that make parity difficult for uniformly activated networks, especially in sparse indirect-encoded substrates.

papers.abstract: Open-ended artificial life systems must acquire diverse competencies from a single evolving genotype. Biological brains combine neuromodulation, which reconfigures circuits without changing connections, with diverse neuron types matched to specific computational roles. Can artificial evolution achieve something analogous in indirectly encoded substrates? Using indirectly encoded substrates evolved via CPPNs, we show through more than 10,000 experiments that neuromodulation alone is insufficient: under evolutionary search, monotonic activation functions impose a 75% ceiling on parity tasks that persists regardless of capacity, topology, or population size. This is an evolutionary search barrier, not a representational limit, since Adam gradient descent achieves 100% on the identical architecture. We combine neuromodulation with per-task activation function selection, matching oscillatory primitives to parity tasks and monotonic to threshold tasks, producing multi-behavioral evolved substrates. The result: 100% simultaneous 5-task success across all 30 seeds (median 14 generations). This generalizes across the oscillatory activation class: all four functions reach 100% (30 seeds each). Neither mechanism suffices alone. The barrier extends to higher-arity and asymmetric tasks, while multi-layer depth provides an alternative path. For open-ended evolution, the computational primitive should itself be an evolvable trait. At inference, one evolved genotype expresses many behaviors.
authors: Romain Claret, Michael O'Neill, Paul Cotofrei, Kilian Stoffel
bullets: Neuromodulation alone reaches a 75% ceiling on parity tasks with monotonic activations, regardless of capacity, topology, or population size.
The ceiling reflects an evolutionary search barrier rather than a representational limit, since gradient descent solves the same architecture perfectly.
Combining neuromodulation with activation selection matches oscillatory functions to parity and monotonic functions to threshold tasks.
The combined approach achieved 100% simultaneous success on five tasks across all 30 seeds, with a median of 14 generations.
The finding extends to higher-arity and asymmetric tasks; increased depth offers an alternative route.

figures.caption: Figure 1: One genotype, five phenotypic behaviors. (Left) A single evolved network (2 inputs, N hidden, 1 output) with shared weights. (Right) The same network is evaluated five times with task-specific NT vectors and activation functions. XOR uses sin; all threshold tasks use tanh. NAND and NOR reuse AND and OR profiles with output inversion (ACh=0.0).
Figure 3: 100% simultaneous 5-task success: per-task accuracy across generations. XOR (sin) breaks the 75% ceiling and converges last.

Figure 2: Activation function comparison on XOR (output versus input sum x1 + x2). The monotonic tanh (blue) stays HIGH at the largest sum, where XOR needs LOW, scoring 3/4 (= 75%); the oscillatory sin (orange) returns LOW there, solving XOR (4/4 = 100%).
Table 1: Experiment summary (3,969 baseline + 6,570 robustness = 10,539 total).
Table 3: Summary of key results. “Repl.” = number of replications; “Rate” = convergence rate (all tasks ≥98%). p-values: Fisher’s exact test. ϕ̂: Cramér’s V.

Table 2: 2-task convergence rates (≥98%, n=30 per pair). Independent: each task has a unique 4D NT vector (ACh=1.0 for all). Compositional: NAND/NOR reuse AND/OR profiles with ACh=0.0 for output inversion (Eq. 3). Per-task activation eliminates all barriers.

papers.selection_reason: Explores evolutionary methods for control using neuromodulation and activation selection in artificial life systems. Relevant to 'Robot Learning and Manipulation' via evolutionary control strategies.
papers.title: Multi-Behavioral Evolved Substrates Through Neuromodulation and Activation Selection
papers.tldr: Evolving both neuromodulation and task-specific activation functions enables one genotype to express multiple behaviors, overcoming evolutionary barriers that neuromodulation alone cannot.

papers.abstract: Persistent AI agents revise beliefs, consolidate memory, and replace execution substrates. Similar successor states can accompany differently authorized transition claims, while legitimate development can change state substantially. We introduce the Cognitive Continuity Test (CCT), a policy-relative contract for verifying submitted transitions using scoped authority, provenance, deterministic application, semantic predicates, and candidate-persistence receipts. CCT distinguishes verified admissibility, affirmative violation, and unresolved required evidence. Separation results concern transition claims rather than live runtime identity; soundness is conditional on the specified checker and evaluator assumptions. IdentityLineageBench provides 24 generated transition families. The reference post-resolution verifier matches all 576 canonical held-out labels; lexical state similarity and a lineage-only diagnostic baseline admit 60.0% and 80.0% of invalid fixtures. These comparisons establish synthetic conformance, not superiority to a policy-aware deployed system. Signed adversarial regressions cover fabricated interaction counts, unsupported belief changes, and mixed missing/contradictory evidence. SIT behavior and actual model migration remain unmeasured. An 18,000-execution valid-path study measures a 6.21 ms default median on resident inputs. We specify the additional activation and recovery obligations needed for deployment.
authors: Jun He, Deying Yu
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of distinguishing legitimate development from unauthorized or unsupported state changes.
Uses scoped authority, provenance, deterministic application, semantic predicates, and candidate-persistence receipts.
Classifies transitions as verified admissible, affirmative violations, or unresolved due to missing required evidence.
On 576 canonical held-out synthetic labels, the reference verifier matched all labels; lexical similarity and lineage-only baselines accepted many invalid fixtures.
Reports a 6.21 ms default median on resident inputs across 18,000 valid-path executions, while SIT behavior and actual model migration remain unmeasured.

papers.abstract: Agent developers increasingly compare prompts, tools, policies, and diagnosis algorithms through simulator-grounded verifiers. A verifier can nevertheless make a solver comparison vacuous: if its probes or predicates encode the target identity, an exact optimizer may appear effective without resolving any genuine ambiguity. We report such a failure in an aggregate-trace debugger for a closed-loop decision agent. Exact minimum hitting set (MHS) and a propagation-aware greedy method returned identical supports in 12/12 development cases and the same planted-fault recovery in 9/12. A subsequent audit found that exact-anchor predicates produced the planted pair in 9/9 cases. After removing those anchors, overall planted-pair recovery was 8/9; hard-probe singleton pairs nevertheless matched the planted pair in 9/9, and no case retained a nonempty residual conflict family after propagation (0/9). The optimizer was correct, but the verifier had already disclosed the answer. We replace solver-first evaluation with a support-gated verification contract. A clean reference map must first show repeated component exposure; a matched reference/current gate must then establish comparable runtime evidence; only afterward may an independently calibrated signal rule return a detection. In a preregistered heldout comprising 1,440 cases and 21,600 partition rows, 55/72 regime-component units passed the reference gate, 54/55 passed the runtime gate, and stable false admission was 0/20 represented components with a one-sided exact 95% upper bound of 0.1391. Within admitted units, affected clean traffic predicted detection better than nominal fault-cell fraction. The main lesson is structural: verify evidence eligibility and non-revelation before optimizing the component selector. Otherwise a stronger solver can merely certify a stronger verifier artifact.
authors: Peiying Zhu, Sidi Chang
bullets: Exact minimum hitting set and propagation-aware greedy produced identical supports in all 12 development cases, but audits showed anchor predicates directly encoded the planted fault pair.
Removing anchors yielded 8/9 planted-pair recovery overall; hard-probe singleton pairs still matched 9/9, with no residual conflict families after propagation.
The proposed support-gated contract requires a clean reference map, matched reference/current runtime evidence, and an independently calibrated detection rule before selection.
In held-out evaluation, 55/72 units passed the reference gate and 54/55 passed the runtime gate; stable false admission was observed in 0/20 represented components.
Within admitted units, affected clean traffic predicted detection better than nominal fault-cell fraction.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses closed-loop agent debugging and verification, introducing a 'support-gated verification contract' to prevent information leakage. Relevant to agent optimization and safety at test time.
papers.title: A Verifier Can Leak the Answer: Diagnosability Before Optimization in Closed-Loop Agent Debugging
papers.tldr: A verifier can reveal the fault before optimization, making solver comparisons meaningless; debugging should first establish evidence eligibility and non-revelation.

papers.abstract: In real-world clinical practice, medical images face open-world shifts: (i) long-tailed rare diseases, (ii) subtle lesions dominated by normal anatomy, and (iii) hierarchical taxonomies. Yet most open-world paradigms assume flat, balanced label spaces, leaving these biomedical demands unresolved. We introduce Generalized Biomedicine Discovery (GBD) and a unified benchmark spanning long-tail, anomaly, and taxonomy-aware discovery. Our key insight is that dominant known patterns form a visual manifold that masks subtle novelty. Inspired by expert diagnosis, we propose SCAN (Surprise-evoked Complementary AccommodatioN), which follows a cognition-inspired perceptual progression: it applies predictive suppression to filter expected norms, triggers surprise-evoked salience to highlight unexpected deviations, and performs complementary accommodation to integrate these shifts into global representations. Extensive experiments show that SCAN improves novel concept discovery while generally preserving established clinical knowledge, and it plugs into existing architectures to better navigate the known-unknown trade-off in medical imaging. Code is available at https://github.com/lytang63/generalized-biomedicine-discovery.
authors: Luyao Tang, Yingkai Yang, Hanqi Chen, Jiewei Zheng, Chaoqi Chen, Cheng Chen
bullets: Addresses three clinical challenges: long-tailed rare diseases, subtle lesions obscured by normal anatomy, and hierarchical label taxonomies.
Introduces SCAN, a cognition-inspired method using predictive suppression, surprise-driven salience, and complementary accommodation.
Benchmarks open-world biomedical discovery across long-tail, anomaly, and taxonomy-aware settings.
Experiments show improved novel concept discovery while generally preserving established clinical knowledge.
SCAN integrates with existing architectures to navigate the trade-off between known and unknown concepts.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Method overview of SCAN (Surprise-evoked Complementary AccommodatioN) for GBD. SCAN refines representations in three steps: (I) it learns a notion of dominant evidence and suppresses predictable visual patterns to expose residual signals; (II) it scores the residuals by “surprise” to highlight sparse, high-energy deviations and aggregates them into salient evidence; (III) it converts the salient evidence into a complementary update and injects it through a gated fusion, limiting disruption to known concepts while strengthening novel structure.

Fig. 1: GBD in practice. Real biomedical data shift beyond the closed world: standard classification fails on unseen diseases, OSR merges heterogeneous novelties into one “unknown”, and conventional discovery often assumes unlabeled data contains only new categories. GBD formalizes three realistic discovery regimes: (I) long-tail rare disease discovery among common cases, (II) normal-to-abnormal discovery of subtle lesions dominated by normal anatomy, and (III) within-taxonomy discovery that uncovers new sibling subtypes to refine diagnostic hierarchies.
Fig. 3: Training dynamics on Gastrovision (Setting I): Known/Novel accuracy and the evolution of the surprise signal (S) and knownness (k) for SelEx and SelEx+SCAN.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes SCAN, a method for open-world medical image discovery that handles long-tail and anomaly detection, relevant to 3D foundation models and spatial intelligence in medical imaging.
papers.title: Generalized Biomedicine Discovery
papers.tldr: GBD introduces a unified framework and benchmark for discovering rare, subtle, and hierarchically organized medical findings under open-world shifts.

papers.abstract: Model judges now supervise multimodal systems at scale, filtering training data, selecting outputs, and supplying the reward that shapes multimodal reasoning models. Trusting one means first checking that it uses its evidence, and that check is itself worth scrutinizing, so we ask whether a counterfactual probe of visual grounding measures what it claims to. The probe edits the image so the ground truth flips, holds the reasoning trace fixed, and asks whether the verdict follows. We formalize it as the Verdict Grounding Score and show it cannot be read the way such scores are read. A verdict responds only to an edit that reaches the judge's decision-relevant reading, so the score is capped by how perceptible the edit is, and unless editing makes the attribute easier to read, the error is one-sided: the score can only make a judge look less grounded than it is. The practical failure is therefore a false alarm, an auditor discarding a usable overseer. Under assumptions we state, we show this missing quantity is not merely bounded but identified from three quantities the same audit protocol already collects, which makes the false-alarm rate directly measurable rather than merely a concern. Auditing nine judges, we find the predicted ordering holds strictly across our entire primary pool, and the typical judge there acts on only about half of the edits whose attribute it can otherwise resolve. Applying a conservative rejection threshold certifies several cells as false alarms outright, the clearest being a judge that detects the injected error essentially every time while still scoring as if it had not used the image at all. The rule that follows is that an image-side counterfactual score should never be reported alone: a detection probe on the unedited image upper-bounds it, certifies its false alarms, and costs nothing extra to run.
authors: Rasul Khanbayov, Hasan Kurban
bullets: The Verdict Grounding Score edits images to flip the ground truth while holding the reasoning trace fixed, then checks whether the verdict changes.

Under stated assumptions, the true perceptibility quantity is identifiable from three measurements already collected by the audit protocol.
Across nine judges, the predicted ordering holds throughout the primary pool; typical judges act on roughly half of otherwise resolvable edits.

papers.selection_reason: Identifies a perceptibility confound in multimodal oversight by analyzing the reliability of model judges, providing a methodological contribution to auditing VLMs.
papers.title: A Low Grounding Score Is Not an Ungrounded Judge: Identifying the Perceptibility Confound in Multimodal Oversight
papers.tldr: Counterfactual visual-grounding scores can falsely label multimodal judges as ungrounded because they confound evidence use with edit perceptibility.

papers.abstract: Belief-based agent memory needs reliable decisions about current state, yet its evidence may be noisy, copied, or stale. Must a memory calibrate its sources before it can improve its decisions? We separate learning, calibration, and revision certification. On one four-model hidden Markov family, learning an unknown Bayes decision requires Theta(l^-2) records and certifying its improvement over an informative incumbent takes O(l^-2) fresh records from the same observation law, while fixed-precision source estimation requires Theta(l^-4) as persistence l vanishes. Thus learning and certifying useful decisions can require quadratically fewer records than source calibration. A broader model class retains the decision rate and source lower bound. Under an unknown identity-plus-background report channel, we characterize the sharp identified interval for policy improvement and derive a finite-sample certificate using observable witness regions, without pure-class anchors. A robustness extension tolerates bounded history-dependent misspecification and conditional copying; split-trained witnesses apply to arbitrary history spaces with explicit power conditions. We integrate policy-bound receipts with Nous Dimensions and test 45,000 held-out mutable-state histories and 9,000 episodes in three external MiniGrid memory environments with an introduced noisy-report interface. The new certificate accepts 9/9 improvements over a constant incumbent and 4/9 over last-write-wins, versus none for the earlier certificate in MiniGrid. Strong established inference baselines remain competitive or better. The result is a statistical account of when memory decisions can be learned and justified without recovering source reliability, not a universally superior memory algorithm.
authors: Pranav Singh
bullets: Separates decision learning, source calibration, and certification of policy improvement.
On a four-model hidden Markov family, decision learning and improvement certification require Θ(l⁻²) records, versus Θ(l⁻⁴) for fixed-precision source estimation as persistence l decreases.
Provides sharp policy-improvement identification intervals and finite-sample certificates under unknown identity-plus-background reporting, without pure-class anchors.
Extends certification to bounded history-dependent misspecification and conditional copying using split-trained witnesses.
In evaluations, the new certificate accepted all 9/9 improvements over a constant incumbent and 4/9 over last-write-wins; established inference baselines remained competitive or better.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a method for learning and certifying memory decisions in embodied environments (MiniGrid) without full source calibration. Strongly aligns with 'Test-Time Learning' and 'Embodied Memory'.
papers.title: Nous: Learning and Certifying Memory Decisions Before Source Calibration
papers.tldr: Memory policies can be learned and their improvements certified with far fewer records than needed to calibrate noisy information sources, under explicit statistical assumptions.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong general capabilities, yet their parameters typically remain fixed after deployment, limiting learning from new interactions. In open-ended environments, this motivates self-evolving agents that continually update reusable state-including model parameters, memories, tool definitions, skills, and workflows-from data, feedback, and accumulated experience. This shift changes the safety problem: once experience becomes reusable state, past events become future causes, and information harmless in one context may later influence decisions with greater persistence, authority, or scope. Self-evolving agent safety therefore asks not only whether a response is aligned or an action authorized, but whether safety properties survive the accumulation, generalization, and cross-context reuse of locally useful experience. We introduce SAVER, a transition-centered framework in which Substrate locates reusable influence, Adaptation captures how it changes, Violation identifies compromised safety attributes, Exposure marks where failures become observable, and Response assesses containment, repair, or revocation. Our survey reveals that failures need not originate from harmful information: legitimate state can become unsafe when adaptation expands its persistence, authority, or scope beyond the conditions under which it was valid. Existing work provides comparatively strong evidence for admission, retrieval, activation, exposure, and local containment, but much less for descendant repair and evaluation after adaptation resumes. We therefore argue for longitudinal evaluation that traces unsafe influence to its originating transition, verifies repair across descendants, and tests whether it can re-emerge under continued evolution.
authors: Jiahao Chen, Zhou Feng, Oubo Ma, Yichen Yan, Ruixiao Lin, Hangtao Zhang, Linkang Du, Hengyu An, Yong Yang, Jun Liu, Junhao Li, Naen Xu, Chunyi Zhou, Yuan Su, Zehao Jin, Qianli Ma, Leyi Qi, Yiming Wang, Zhe Ma, Yuwen Pu, Mengyao Du, Yuanyi Song, Enhao Huang, Zhihui Fu, Jun Wang, Jinfeng Li, Yuefeng Chen, Hui Xue, Yiming Li, Tianyu Du, Shouling Ji
bullets: Self-evolving agents update parameters, memories, tools, skills, or workflows from ongoing experience, making past events potential future causes.
The SAVER framework analyzes safety through Substrate, Adaptation, Violation, Exposure, and Response.
Legitimate information can become unsafe if adaptation expands its persistence, authority, or scope beyond its original context.
Existing research covers admission, retrieval, activation, exposure, and local containment more strongly than descendant repair or post-repair evaluation.
The survey advocates longitudinal testing that traces unsafe influence, verifies repair across descendants, and checks for re-emergence during continued evolution.

papers.selection_reason: Surveys safety in self-evolving agents, focusing on state accumulation and cross-context reuse. Relevant to the 'Continual and Online Learning' subtopic regarding how agents adapt and retain state.
papers.title: Safety in Self-Evolving Agents: A Survey

papers.abstract: Humans express uncertainty verbally via markers (e.g., "possible," "likely"), yet most LLM uncertainty quantification (UQ) relies on costing likelihood- or consistency-based signals. From a cognitive perspective, accurate verbal uncertainty reflects metacognitive monitoring, representing knowledge boundaries ("knowing that you don't know") to support regulation and information seeking. In this paper, we investigate how LLMs diverge from humans in verbal uncertainty quantification and whether verbal markers can reliably quantify LLM uncertainty. We curate a corpus of human uncertainty markers from psychology and decision-science literature and benchmark LLMs against it. We observe that LLMs encode verbal uncertainty with numerical levels that differ substantially from those of humans. We then introduce METHODNAME, a novel optimization-based algorithm that learns an optimal uncertainty profile over uncertainty markers directly from LLM outputs. By fitting a marker-uncertainty mapping to best explain empirical correctness, METHODNAME discovers how much probability mass each verbal marker should convey, rather than estimating uncertainty via repeated sampling. METHODNAME enables a direct, marker-level comparison of confidence semantics between humans and LLMs, disentangling mismatch and revealing systematic confidence disparities in verbal expressions.
authors: Jinhao Duan, Zicheng Liu, Zijie Liu, Kaidi Xu, Tianlong Chen
bullets: Studies whether phrases such as “likely” and “possible” reliably quantify LLM uncertainty.
Builds a corpus of human uncertainty markers from psychology and decision-science research for benchmarking.
Finds substantial differences between LLM and human numerical interpretations of verbal uncertainty.
Introduces METHODNAME, an optimization-based method that learns uncertainty profiles for markers directly from LLM outputs.
The method avoids repeated sampling and exposes systematic confidence disparities between human and LLM expressions.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Comparison of traditional uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods and our method VOCAL. Traditional UQ methods (samplingbased and logits-based) exhibit a gap with human uncertainty expressions. In VOCAL, UM-lookup tables derived from human data alone cannot fully capture model uncertainty, so they are optimized with the model’s confidence distribution to better align with its internal uncertainty expressions.

Figure 5. The evaluation results of VOCAL and multi-sample based UQ methods. It is worth noting that sampling-based methods rely on semantic consistency calculations, which are expensive and introduce latency in real-world deployment. It is shown that VOCAL achieves comparable performance to sampling-based UQ methods.

Figure 3. The distributions of uncertainty markers expressed by LLMs. We show that advanced LLMs, such as GPT-4o, express uncertainty in a more diverse manner compared to small LLMs (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct). This also reveals that small LLMs tend to be over confident.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates LLMs' internal representation of linguistic uncertainty and introduces a method to map verbal markers to uncertainty levels, contributing to the understanding of LLM confidence and reasoning.
papers.title: "very likely" Means "uncertain"? How LLMs Diverge from Humans in Linguistic Uncertainty Quantification
papers.tldr: LLMs assign substantially different meanings to verbal uncertainty markers than humans, motivating METHODNAME to learn marker-level confidence from empirical correctness.

papers.abstract: Reliable visual inspection is essential for quality assurance in aero-engine blade manufacturing, where defect appearance may vary across production lines, imaging conditions, blade poses, and surface backgrounds. Such domain shifts cause a mismatch between training and deployment data and degrade the reliability of deep defect detectors in online inspection. This problem is particularly challenging because aero-engine blade images usually contain sparse defects, making pseudolabel-based adaptation vulnerable to noisy or missing predictions. To address this issue, we propose Aero-engine Blade Defect Detector (ABDD), an online adaptive detection framework based on test-time adaptation. ABDD introduces a Dual-Alignment Strategy to jointly adapt global visual style and local defect morphology by combining feature-statistics alignment with pseudo-box alignment. To reduce error accumulation from unreliable pseudo labels, an Uncertainty-aware Box Filtering mechanism evaluates pseudo boxes using classification confidence, classification entropy, and localization entropy. In addition, a lightweight Sparse Dilated Mona module enables parameter-efficient delta tuning while limiting source-domain forgetting. ABDD is evaluated on CD-AeBD and HD-AeBD under multiple domain-shift scenarios, with TTA strategies compared under a unified RT-DETR + Swin-T architecture. Experiments show that ABDD consistently improves detection robustness under domain shifts, and its practicality is further validated on an industrial inspection platform.
authors: Zhaoyang Wang, Haiyong Chen, Dongying Li, Yining Wang, Huapeng Wu, Xinwei Lv, Atik Shahariar
bullets: Addresses degradation caused by varying production lines, imaging conditions, blade poses, and surface backgrounds.
Aligns global visual statistics and local defect morphology using feature-statistics and pseudo-box alignment.
Filters unreliable pseudo boxes using classification confidence, classification entropy, and localization entropy.
Uses a lightweight Sparse Dilated Mona module for parameter-efficient adaptation with reduced source-domain forgetting.
Evaluations on CD-AeBD and HD-AeBD show consistently improved robustness, with additional validation on an industrial inspection platform.

papers.abstract: Assembly actions are compositional: they combine a manipulation with a part or tool. In deployment, systems routinely encounter novel combinations of familiar components, yet an atomic action classifier assigns every unseen combination exactly zero probability by construction. The prevailing solution is verb--noun decomposition, which predicts components separately and recombines them to reach unseen actions. While widely adopted, how decomposition generalizes under compositional shift remains poorly understood. We present a systematic analysis of verb--noun decomposition across three assembly datasets (MECCANO, HAViD, and IMPACT). Although decomposition escapes the atomic ceiling, its generalization extends only partially beyond it. Unseen-composition performance remains strongly tied to the co-occurrence structure of the training data, indicating that much of the observed gain arises from interpolation within densely supported regions of the compositional space rather than from unconstrained recombination. Across datasets, failures consistently concentrate on the larger-vocabulary component, and IMPACT's verb-heavy vocabulary reverses the bottleneck from nouns to verbs. We further show that shared-encoder training introduces component entanglement, encouraging reliance on co-occurrence patterns that transfer poorly to unseen compositions and trailing independent recombination by up to $6.0\times$ in harmonic mean. Taken together, these findings explain why decomposition achieves only partial compositional generalization in practice. By identifying primitive support, vocabulary asymmetry, and component entanglement as connected sources of error, we provide a portable diagnostic framework for studying compositional recognition beyond aggregate accuracy. Code: https://github.com/hisalaheiyo/assembly.
authors: Changyi Li, Yu Xiao
bullets: Atomic classifiers assign zero probability to unseen verb–noun combinations, motivating compositional decomposition.
Across MECCANO, HAViD, and IMPACT, decomposition surpasses this atomic ceiling but generalizes only partially beyond supported combinations.
Errors concentrate on the component with the larger vocabulary; IMPACT reverses the usual noun bottleneck because it has more verbs.
Shared-encoder training promotes co-occurrence-based component entanglement and can trail independent recombination by up to 6.0× in harmonic mean.
The study proposes diagnostics based on primitive support, vocabulary asymmetry, and component entanglement.

Failures consistently concentrate on the largervocabulary component. (b) The verb bottleneck in IMPACT persists across all five views, indicating that the asymmetry follows vocabulary structure rather than viewpoint.

Figure 2: Unseen accuracy increasingly follows primitive support as the composition grid becomes denser. Each point is an unseen verb–noun pair. Correlation strength rises from MECCANO to IMPACT to HAViD, mirroring the density of the observed composition grid. High-support pairs achieve the strongest performance, whereas low-support pairs remain near zero.

Figure 4: More factorization does not imply better compositional generalization. HAViD performance under k = 1 . . .4 factorization levels. The standard two-component decomposition (k = 2) achieves the best unseen performance. Further factorization recovers seen accuracy but degrades generalization. Inset: the corresponding k=1→2 transition on MECCANO and IMPACT.

C2C substantially improves the shared baseline but adds little once components are already trained independently.

Figure 6: Remaining headroom is largely a ranking problem. Unseen action top-K under the same scoring function used in Table 2. Atomic prediction remains at zero for all K, whereas decomposition frequently ranks the correct unseen composition within its top candidates despite low top-1 accuracy.

Table 3: The bottleneck follows vocabulary size rather than component identity. Across datasets, unseen failures consistently concentrate on the larger-vocabulary component. IMPACT reverses the common noun-heavy regime, and the bottleneck reverses with it across all five views.

Table 2: Performance on the compositional split. Seen and unseen action top-1 accuracy and harmonic mean (HM) for five recognition formulations across three datasets. Atomic prediction serves as the unreachable baseline, while shared and independent decomposition make unseen compositions reachable. This table provides the reference point for all subsequent analyses.

Table 5: Finer factorization does not improve compositional generalization. The standard two-component decomposition (k = 2) provides the best unseen performance. Increasing granularity mainly improves seen accuracy while degrading transfer to unseen compositions.

Table 1: Structural diversity of the datasets used in this study. IMPACT uniquely reverses the common noun-heavy regime, enabling a direct test of whether the bottleneck follows vocabulary size rather than component type.

Table 4: Evidence for component entanglement in shared training. The shortcut score ∆ measures the excess seen-to-unseen drop of a jointly trained component head relative to its independently trained counterpart. Large ∆ values together with near-zero seen margins indicate that shared training provides little benefit on seen compositions while substantially increasing the unseen generalization gap.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes verb-noun decomposition in assembly action recognition, providing insights into generalization limits for robotic manipulation tasks.
papers.title: Reachability Is Not Generalization: Understanding Verb--Noun Decomposition in Assembly Action Recognition
papers.tldr: Verb–noun decomposition helps recognize unseen assembly actions, but its generalization is largely limited by training co-occurrences, vocabulary imbalance, and entanglement between components.

papers.abstract:
Four-bit floating-point (FP4) Tensor Cores accelerate matrix multiplication, but scale computation, operand packing, layout construction, and saved backward state can erase the gain. We present \emph{format-aware fusion}, which co-designs each quantization producer with its scale domain and consumer layout for native \mxfp{}, global 
vfp{}, and cooperative-thread-array-local 
vfp{}. We evaluate Llama-3-family 8B pretraining through 160 billion tokens using bfloat16 output projections and compiled cross entropy. In matched same-accelerator probes, bfloat16 and Transformer Engine 
vfp{} reach 18.8K and 27.6K tokens/s/GPU, while our fastest custom route reaches 37.9K. \mxfp{} with row-gradient stochastic rounding and fixed-sign 32-value Hadamard weight-gradient preconditioning reaches 37.2K tokens/s/GPU (86.3\% bfloat16 model FLOP utilization) and ends 2.11\% above the raw bfloat16 training-loss endpoint. A Transformer Engine recipe with four final bfloat16 blocks ends 0.87\% above bfloat16 at 27.1K tokens/s/GPU. Downstream rankings differ from training-loss rankings, showing that FP4 outcomes depend jointly on scale contract, operand, and execution path.
authors: Robert Hu
bullets: FP4 speedups can be lost to scale computation, operand packing, layout construction, and backward-state storage.
The method co-designs quantization producers with scale domains and consumer layouts for native MXFP, global NVFP, and CTA-local NVFP.
On Llama-3-family 8B pretraining over 160B tokens, the fastest custom route reaches 37.9K tokens/s/GPU versus 18.8K for bfloat16 and 27.6K for Transformer Engine NVFP.
MXFP with stochastic row-gradient rounding and Hadamard weight-gradient preconditioning achieves 37.2K tokens/s/GPU and ends 2.11% above the raw bfloat16 training-loss endpoint.
Downstream rankings differ from training-loss rankings, indicating FP4 quality depends on the scale contract, operands, and execution path.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Scale-completion boundaries for the three custom routes. MXFP4 finalizes a local 32-value scale; global NVFP4 waits for tensor amax; CTA-local NVFP4 computes tile-owned row and column outer factors without waiting for a tensor-wide reduction. The completion point determines which preparation work can be fused with its matrix multiplication.

Figure 4: Formats and packed views for the plain-H16 operand hybrid. Here r and c denote the consumer-facing row- and column-packed scale/layout representations; they do not change a tensor’s logical shape. Top: Fprop consumes row-facing X and W , Dgrad consumes row-facing dY and column-facing W , and Wgrad consumes column-facing dY and X. Bottom: Fprop uses MXFP4 Xr and 2D32 Wr; Dgrad uses CTA-local NVFP4 dYr with row stochastic rounding (SR) and 2D16 Wc; Wgrad uses MXFP4 dYc and Xc with paired plain-H16 preconditioning. One fused backward producer emits both dY representations from the BF16 tile. Wgrad does not read W because it produces dW . Plain H16 has no sign flips; fixed H32 changes only the paired Wgrad preconditioner.

Figure 3: Tensor-global and CTA-local NVFP4 outer-scale domains. Global NVFP4 gates block packing on tensor amax. Our CTA-local route carries tile-owned row and column outer factors through the full K accumulation and applies αiβj once in the epilogue.

Figure 1: Operand-specific E8M0 scale selection. Encode-centric scaling rounds the block maximum upward and keeps every input within the E2M1 endpoint. For a non-power-of-two maximum, decodecentric scaling rounds downward, halves the decoded grid spacing, and clips the block tail. Our route applies this range–resolution choice per operand: activations and gradients use the encode-centric rule, while 2D32 weights select the finer scale only under the fixed aT /sT < 0.87 condition.

Figure 5: Independent one-dimensional scales can make Fprop and Dgrad consume different numerical weights. Orientation-consistent 2D quantization computes one tile encoding and exposes it through row- and column-oriented memory layouts. Our implementation optimization fuses production of those layouts into the custom MXFP4 and CTA-local producers under their respective scale policies.

Figure 8: Training loss from 120B to 160B tokens. Diamonds mark exact logged endpoints. As in Figure 7, the late custom-global-NVFP4 markers are exact observations and the dashed curve is a smoothed visual guide, not additional measurements.

Figure 6: Serial and format-aware execution of the QKV and gated-FFN boundaries. Solid boxes and arrows show values produced and consumed within one execution boundary; they do not imply one monolithic kernel. Purple dashed arrows show stream overlap. Distributed collectives remain separate operations even when their launch overlaps local work. In panels B and D, row stochastic rounding (SR) applies only to the gradient view consumed by Dgrad; a paired fixed-sign Hadamard transform (H), when enabled, applies to both column operands consumed by Wgrad.

Figure 7: Llama-8B training loss and relative difference from the BF16 reference. Continuous histories use EMA-31, and diamonds mark the final plotted endpoint. Custom-global-NVFP4 has regular observations through step 19,000, but its dense later history was not retained. The upper panel therefore shows the 74 exact later observations recovered from training logs, including the terminal diamond; the lower panel shows the 18 observations recorded at the same step as BF16. The dashed custom-global-NVFP4 line is a smoothed visual guide through those sparse observations, not additional measurements. Appendix C records the surviving data sources.

papers.selection_reason: Focuses on optimizing FP4 quantization and pretraining efficiency, specifically addressing memory layout and backward state optimization, which directly relates to memory efficiency in large-scale model training.
papers.title: Format-Aware Fusion for Fast FP4 Pretraining
papers.tldr: Format-aware fusion makes FP4 pretraining substantially faster by jointly designing quantization scales, layouts, and execution paths while preserving near-bfloat16 quality.

papers.abstract: Graphics processing unit (GPU) generations scale matrix, special-function, and memory pipelines at different rates, so kernel bottlenecks move as hardware evolves. FlashAttention-4 exposed this imbalance inside attention on NVIDIA Blackwell. We test whether short polynomial programs can accelerate other special-function-unit (SFU) operations in large language models (LLMs). We first compare native PyTorch evaluation with packed fused multiply--add (FMA) programs in an isolated IEEE binary16 (FP16) sweep spanning L2-resident and high-bandwidth-memory (HBM)-resident working sets. We then replace native sigmoid, tanh, and sigmoid linear unit (SiLU) with degree-3 or degree-4 bfloat16 (BF16) programs in four GB200 integration tasks: dense SiLU, tanh-softcapped attention, sigmoid attention, and routed-expert Swish-gated linear unit (SwiGLU). The programs combine analytical symmetry, target-format rounding, and packed arithmetic inside consuming kernels. The isolated paths improve by 1.19--2.19x in L2 and 1.00--1.70x in HBM. The dense-SiLU, tanh-softcapped-attention, and routed-expert substitutions improve complete training-step throughput by 2.7\%, 2.9\%, and 8.0\%, respectively. The sigmoid-attention substitution improves complete-attention forward by 7.4\% and the complete GPU step by 0.3\%. Same-checkpoint open-weight ablations and one paired pre-training comparison per task extend the evaluation to model behavior. At common horizons near 100 billion tokens, the final smoothed training-loss differences (polynomial minus native) range from $-0.107$ to $+0.079$ across the four tasks.
authors: Robert Hu
bullets: GPU pipeline imbalances make special-function operations potential bottlenecks as hardware evolves.
The approach uses degree-3/4 BF16 polynomial programs with symmetry, target-format rounding, packed arithmetic, and fusion into consuming kernels.
Isolated FP16 kernels improve by 1.19–2.19× in L2-resident settings and up to 1.70× for HBM-resident settings.
End-to-end gains reach 8.0% for routed-expert SwiGLU, with 2.7–2.9% gains for dense SiLU and tanh-softcapped attention; sigmoid attention gains 7.4% in forward and 0.3% per GPU step.
Across four tasks, loss differences versus native functions range from −0.107 to +0.079 near 100B tokens, indicating task-dependent behavioral differences.

papers.selection_reason: Polynomial approximations for GPU special-function units to accelerate LLM training, a direct efficiency contribution.
papers.title: Fast Polynomial Transcendentals for LLMs
papers.tldr: Short, packed polynomial approximations can accelerate LLM sigmoid, tanh, and SiLU operations on NVIDIA GB200 GPUs while preserving broadly similar training behavior.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting have enabled open-vocabulary and referring segmentation by distilling semantic knowledge from 2D foundation models into 3D representations. However, existing referring fields embed language features in a globally view-invariant space, making them fundamentally unable to resolve observer-centric spatial relations (e.g., "to the left of") that depend on camera pose. We propose DSSR-3D, an inference-time framework for view-dependent referring segmentation on continuous 3D Gaussian fields, formalized as two interfaces - pose-invariant semantic localization and pose-conditioned spatial reasoning - such that any pair of functions satisfying these constraints yields a valid instantiation, requiring no retraining of the underlying semantic field and no reliance on discrete geometric proxies such as bounding boxes. We instantiate the two interfaces with a temperature-sharpened softmax localization mechanism and a projection-based directional scoring function, fused via a lightweight, training-free step, and show they transfer zero-shot to structurally distinct semantic fields without adaptation. We further propose ViewRef-GS, a benchmark isolating view-dependent segmentation on 3D Gaussian fields, evaluated jointly with an augmented Ref-LERF to provide a comprehensive testbed for viewpoint-dependent spatial grounding. Experiments show consistent gains over existing 3DGS-based referring methods, with no additional training beyond the base semantic field
authors: Thanh-Khoi Nguyen, Thien-Phuc Tran, Minh-Triet Tran
bullets: Addresses the inability of globally view-invariant semantic fields to interpret observer-centric relations such as “to the left of.”
Decouples pose-invariant semantic localization from pose-conditioned spatial reasoning through two general interfaces.
Instantiates the framework with temperature-sharpened softmax localization and projection-based directional scoring, fused without retraining or bounding boxes.
Transfers zero-shot across structurally distinct semantic fields and consistently improves over existing 3DGS referring methods.
Introduces ViewRef-GS and an augmented Ref-LERF evaluation setup for viewpoint-dependent spatial grounding.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes DSSR-3D for view-dependent referring segmentation in 3D Gaussians, explicitly addressing pose-conditioned spatial reasoning and spatial localization.
papers.title: DSSR-3D: Decoupled Reasoning for View-Dependent Referring in 3D Gaussians
papers.tldr: DSSR-3D enables training-free, view-dependent referring segmentation in 3D Gaussian fields by separating semantic localization from camera-aware spatial reasoning.

papers.abstract: Street-view imagery is increasingly used to infer urban attributes, but predictive accuracy alone does not reveal how much a photograph contributes beyond data already available for the same place. We compare image-based predictions with existing urban data across seven attributes from five public resources and three VLMs. The same urban units are evaluated using images, task context, nearby observations, and public records, while image replacements and conflicting records test source reliance. Existing urban data matched or exceeded image-only models for road damage, curb ramps, and house price, while neighbouring official statistics nearly matched the best image result for population. Images were more informative for building type, building function, and low-rise floor count. For floor count, image advantage increased by 5.7 percentage points per doubling of distance to the nearest labelled building and declined for tall buildings whose rooflines often fell outside the frame. Models frequently followed conflicting records. OpenFACADES floor annotations were generated with OpenStreetMap floor values and showed the opposite height-dependent error pattern from image-only reruns. Street-view image value therefore depends on visual legibility and local data coverage. Comparing images with existing urban data can guide image collection and clarify the provenance of derived urban maps.
authors: Kaizhen Tan
bullets: Compares three VLMs using street-view images, task context, nearby observations, and public records across seven urban attributes.
Existing data matched or exceeded image-only models for road damage, curb ramps, and house price; nearby statistics nearly matched image performance for population.
Images were more informative for building type, building function, and low-rise floor count.
For floor count, image advantage grew with distance from labelled buildings but declined for tall buildings whose rooflines were often out of frame.
Models often followed conflicting records, highlighting the importance of visual legibility, local data coverage, and source provenance.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates the utility of VLMs for urban sensing by comparing street-view imagery predictions against existing urban data, focusing on spatial understanding.
papers.title: Seeing the City or Recognizing the Place? What Street-View Imagery Adds Beyond Existing Urban Data in VLM Urban Sensing
papers.tldr: Street-view images add the most value for visually legible building attributes, while existing urban data can match or outperform them for several other urban-sensing tasks.

papers.abstract: Across three vision-language model architectures (LLaVA-1.5-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL3-8B), we report a universal negative finding for mid-layer interpretability. On POPE -- the benchmark common to all three -- the mid layers encode the ground-truth answer in 68-91% of errors, yet this signal is not causally active for the final prediction: residual-stream patching yields 0% non-trivial flip at the layer level on all three architectures, and on two of three at the per-head level (Qwen: 0/12,600 patched forwards). The lone exception, InternVL3 layer-20 head-2, is a non-vocab, self-attending head whose effect is localized to that specific head (p < 1e-4). Despite the null, the errors separate operationally into three failure modes -- Perception Failure, Encoded-but-Disconnected, Prior-Override -- learnable above 60% on all three architectures, and the architecture's prior direction predicts which of two interventions elicits a category-specific response. We report these mitigation effects under oracle labels as evidence the categories are mechanistically real, not as a deployable method.
authors: Genpei Zhang
bullets: Across LLaVA-1.5-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and InternVL3-8B on POPE, 68–91% of errors encode the ground-truth answer in mid layers.
Layer-level patching produces no non-trivial prediction flips in any architecture; per-head patching is also null for Qwen and one other model.
InternVL3 layer-20 head-2 is a narrow exception, with a localized, statistically significant effect.
Errors separate into Perception Failure, Encoded-but-Disconnected, and Prior-Override, with over-60% learnability across models.
Intervention responses depend on failure category and architecture, but results use oracle labels and are not presented as a deployable mitigation method.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Per-head patching flip-rate heatmaps at the last-text position across the three architectures (shared vmax 30%). The only cell exceeding the layer-level null upper CI is InternVL3 L20 H2 (circled, panel c); LLaVA and Qwen are essentially flat at zero.

Figure 1: Per-category mid-layer top-1 margin distributions across the three architectures (LLaVA L13, Qwen L12, InternVL3 L20). The three failure categories separate by margin shape—broad-tailed (PF), low (EBD), tight near zero (PO)—which is the signal the 24-feature classifier exploits.

Figure 2: Bimodal POPE failure-mode separation across 5 model×benchmark cells: pred=No errors are 95–100% EAS-positive (bottom), pred=Yes are < 5% (top). The split is fixed by prediction direction; the non-trivial content is that the two halves also differ in mid-layer signal.

Figure 4: InternVL3 layer 20 head 2 mechanism triplet (the per-head exception of Figure 3). (a) 5-variant sanity sweep (baseline vs. random, zero, different head, different layer). (b) Vocab projection: yes/no tokens absent from the head’s top-5. (c) Attention: 96% of mass on its own position. Causal but not vocab-encoding, and self-attending.

InternVL3 runs in bfloat16 with eager attention (fp16 produced NaN logits on this architecture); this is a precision/stability choice and does not affect any qualitative conclusion—the layer-level patching null holds identically across all three models regardless of precision.

On prior-dominated architectures a single direction bit is already strong, so the continuous features add the most where the label is not collinear with prediction direction (LLaVA, +20 points).

Table 1: Three-architecture summary of all main-paper results. EAS (POPE): mid-layer top-1 hit rate on POPE errors. Peak band: layers of strongest signal (relative depth). Patching null: per-pair non-trivial flip rate at the layer and per-head levels; InternVL3 L20 H2 is the only tuple rejecting the null. Table 4: Scan window versus peak band. The scan window (wider) defines the EAS condition; the peak band (narrower) carries the strongest signal and fixes the relative depth, computed against the language-model layer count. papers.selection_reason: Investigates interpretability failures in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) by categorizing failure modes (Perception, Encoded-but-Disconnected, Prior-Override) through causal intervention.
papers.title: Encoded but Disconnected: Decomposing Vision-Language Model Failures under a Patching Null
papers.tldr: Mid-layer signals often contain the correct answer in vision-language model errors, but residual-stream patching shows they are generally disconnected from the final prediction; errors nonetheless divide into three mechanistic failure modes.

papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly act through modular systems, such as order, payment, inventory, and shipment services, where actions in one module change which transitions are valid in another. Standard world models usually fit observational traces, but this is not the quantity needed for intervention-time planning: a trace may show that payment precedes shipment without identifying whether payment authorizes shipment, inventory mediates the effect, or a hidden trigger explains both. We study this gap through FedCausalCompose, a causal world-model framework for modular LLM agents in which local actions provide intervention-response evidence for cross-module interfaces. We first show that observational world models incur an irreducible interventional error under unblocked back-door paths, that interface recovery improves with intervention-response coverage, and that an oracle causal composition can beat the non-causal lower bound when coverage and local mechanism errors are controlled. We then test the resulting prediction in diagnostic agent settings. Causal interfaces help most in structured tool environments, where API signatures expose preconditions and downstream effects. In contrast, dialogue and narrative environments often ignore raw edge lists unless a short attention anchor makes the causal information decision-relevant. These results identify a concrete condition for causal world models in LLM agents: causal structure helps when cross-module interfaces are both statistically identifiable and presented in a form the agent can use at action time.
authors: Xinyuan Song, Zekun Cai
bullets: Observational traces alone can leave interventional behavior ambiguous because of unblocked confounding or hidden mechanisms.
FedCausalCompose learns causal interfaces from local intervention-response evidence across modules.
Interface recovery improves with intervention-response coverage, and accurate causal composition can outperform non-causal limits when local errors are controlled.
Causal information helps most in structured tool environments with explicit preconditions and downstream effects.
Dialogue and narrative settings often need a concise attention anchor for agents to use causal edge information at decision time.

figures.caption: Figure 1: FedCausalCompose pipeline. Each functional module contributes local actions, interface events, and intervention-response summaries. The aggregator validates cross-module causal edges and composes them into a global world model without treating all client traces as one undifferentiated sequence.

Figure 2: Back-door gap. Observational sequence models learn µobs, while intervention-time rollouts require µint. The resulting gap grows with confounding strength and compounds across interface hops.

Figure 3: Federated causal loop. Local modules send intervention-response summaries to an aggregator, which updates the interface graph and dispatches causal rollout constraints without centralizing raw trajectories.
Figure 4: Local causal control. A client checks upstream interfaces, predicts downstream effects, gates unsafe actions, and verifies residuals after execution.

Table 1: Key diagnostic findings. We organize results by the empirical question each cell tests. Success values are percentages unless otherwise noted; ROUGE-L is reported for APIBank because it is a standard API-response quality metric.

Table 2: Representative efficiency metrics. Lower cost per successful run is better. The table shows that causal prompting is not free: it helps only when the added structure improves decisions enough to offset longer prompts or extra calls.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces causal world models for modular LLM agents, addressing intervention-time planning and interface recovery, relevant to world-model research.
papers.title: When Do Causal World Models Help Modular LLM Agents
papers.tldr: Causal world models improve modular LLM-agent planning when cross-module effects are identifiable through interventions and presented in an actionable form.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon language agents increasingly rely on external memory as a frozen world model, yet current memory systems are usually judged only by task success or token cost. We argue that the missing object is the shape of memory use: under finite context and repeated retrieval, agent memory can concentrate on a small core while leaving rare states in a long tail where prediction errors accumulate. We study this effect through a conservative tail audit and find that concentration is reproducible but policy-dependent. Random-walk agents produce log-normal-compatible retrieval artifacts, whereas semantic LLM policies yield the strongest truncated-power-law-compatible core--tail traces. Motivated by this audit, we propose Core--Tail World Model (CTWM), a rank-based memory controller that allocates prompt budget with a single exponent $\tau$ while retaining a summarized tail. On Synthetic Graph World, CTWM preserves full state and transition coverage, reduces prompt tokens by 5.9%, and lowers bottom-half tail prediction error by 13.6% relative to a graph-memory baseline. The same paired comparison gives consistent token savings on ALFWorld and a 24.48% token reduction on LongMemEval with aggregate accuracy parity. These results suggest that heavy-tailed memory traces are not only a diagnostic of finite retrieval, but also a practical control signal for token-efficient agent world models.
authors: Xinyuan Song, Zekun Cai
bullets: Memory systems can concentrate on a small core while rare states form a long tail with accumulating prediction errors.
A tail audit finds reproducible, policy-dependent concentration: random walks show log-normal-compatible traces, while semantic LLM policies show stronger truncated-power-law-compatible traces.
CTWM uses rank-based allocation with one exponent to prioritize the core while retaining a summarized tail.
On Synthetic Graph World, CTWM preserves full state and transition coverage, cuts prompt tokens by 5.9%, and reduces bottom-half tail prediction error by 13.6% versus a graph-memory baseline.
It also yields consistent token savings on ALFWorld and cuts LongMemEval tokens by 24.48% with aggregate accuracy parity.

figures.caption: Figure 2: CTWM update and allocation pipeline. Observations are parsed into states and transitions, the finite memory reservoir is ranked for the current step, and the ranked list is partitioned into a high-priority core and summarized tail. The rank exponent controls how much prompt budget each rank receives. Prediction error, retrieval counts, and token usage are logged after each API call, closing the measurement loop used in the experiments.

Figure 3: Retriever ladder for the random-walk control. Each rung removes or changes one mechanism in the memory backend and reports both the access-shape diagnostic and the interpretation. Uniform frequency sorting is already concentrated but graph-decoupled; state-aware top-k retrieval separates topology families; disabling retrieval collapses Gini to 0.29–0.35; and non-preferential retrieval retains most of the concentration. The large drop when retrieval is disabled shows that the random-walk tail is primarily a state-aware finite-retrieval effect, not a property of a power-law environment.

Figure 6: Frozen-trajectory attribution. The retrieval map ρ and ranked memory identifiers are fixed, so verbose and compact encodings share the same backend. What changes is the LLM-facing prompt view: verbose score-heavy triples produce a longer prompt and a different policy-induced trajectory, while compact ranked hints plus a tail summary produce a shorter prompt and lower tail error. Matched replay removes the live gap to within 4× 10−4, attributing the observed difference to the policy path rather than to a changed retrieval function.

Figure 4: Topology evidence under semantic policy. The figure reports fitted tail exponent, bootstrap goodness-of-fit, and likelihood-ratio evidence for four topology families. Gray dashed lines mark audit references in the first two panels: α̂ = 2 and pgof = 0.10. papers.abstract: Frequency-collapse attention [Zeris, 2026e] achieves large gains over standard dot-product attention by replacing the Q/K dot product with a bandpass-filtered inner product at a learned frequency. A natural follow-up question is: which filter shape works best, and why? We test five hypotheses about filter properties -- DC suppression, Nyquist suppression, bandwidth, centre frequency, and multi-scale coverage -- using a controlled ablation on character-level language modelling (TinyShakespeare, 6-layer GPT). Our main findings are: (1) DC and Nyquist components are actively harmful (val ~= 2.0, equivalent to phase randomisation), confirming that oscillatory bandpass structure is essential, not just any low-dimensional spectral summary; (2) the optimal single-scale bandwidth is sigma ~= 2 bins centred at paragraph scale (~70 tokens), giving a clean gain of Delta = +1.15 nats over BASE-DOT; (3) admissible filters (zero-mean, Mexican Hat DOG m = 2) outperform non-admissible Gaussians at the same scale and provide partial protection against bilateral FFT leakage; (4) bilateral FFT leakage scales monotonically with spectral coverage -- narrowband filters (gap > +4) are clean, wideband filters (gap < +2) are leaky; and (5) causal time-domain Morlet at character scale cannot beat BASE-DOT (K=128 taps covers 50% of T=256 context), motivating word-level experiments in the companion MorletQK paper [Zeris, 2026f]. Together, findings (1)-(5) characterise FourierQK as effective in bidirectional attention settings (encoder-style, e.g. BERT), where full-sequence context is available at both training and inference time; autoregressive generation requires a causal spectral variant such as MorletQK [Zeris, 2026f] (decoder-style, e.g. GPT). Code available at: https://github.com/AthanasiosZeris/energy-gated-attention
authors: Athanasios Zeris
bullets: DC and Nyquist components are harmful, showing that useful spectral structure must be oscillatory and bandpass.
A single-scale filter with bandwidth ≈2 bins at paragraph scale (~70 tokens) improves character-level language modeling by Δ=+1.15 nats over dot-product attention.
Admissible zero-mean Mexican Hat (DOG, m=2) filters outperform same-scale Gaussian filters and partially reduce FFT leakage.
Leakage increases with spectral coverage: narrowband filters are cleaner, while wideband filters are leakier.
Causal character-scale Morlet filters do not surpass the baseline, motivating a separate causal spectral approach for autoregressive generation.
